finding: The live range of $1,500-$4,800 is too low at both ends for a remanufactured automatic transmission on the vehicles checked. Built totals (transmission price without the refundable core charge + stated hours x $120-$160/hr, the national middle labor rate used for these checks): economy 2020 Nissan Versa CVT about $4,175-$5,685 (7.5-12 hr); midsize 2021 Honda Accord CVT about $3,816-$6,012 (6.2-12 hr); truck 2021 Silverado 1500 8-speed about $4,847-$5,671 (5.4-7.4 hr); luxury 2021 Cadillac XT4 9-speed about $5,052-$7,647 (12.3 hr; with the front-wheel-drive unit at list, $4,215.61, the top is about $6,184). So every total we can build starts above $3,800 and every class tops out above $5,600; the live ceiling of $4,800 is below the bottom of the truck and luxury classes and below the top of all four. The $1,500 floor is not supported by anything loaded: the cheapest remanufactured unit seen is $3,072 (Honda's own Accord CVT kit at an online discount) before any labor, and the smallest stated labor time is 5.4 hours (about $650 at $120/hr). Benchmarks agree: ConsumerAffairs reports $6,238-$6,764 on average and a shop owner's $3,000-$4,000 even for old four-speed units; Kelley Blue Book says $2,900-$7,100 for a new transmission and $8,143-$8,689 at a dealer for a 2016 Acura MDX. A figure near $1,500 looks like a used (salvage-yard) transmission or a rebuild of a simple older unit, not a remanufactured one. A range of roughly $3,800-$7,600 fits what was found; older four- and five-speed vehicles may come in lower, but only one such price was loaded (a remanufactured 2003 Accord 5-speed at $3,499 before labor). What changed on the 2026-11-20 second look: the luxury example was switched from the 2016 Acura MDX to the 2021 Cadillac XT4, because neither MDX labor figure was a time for replacing the transmission alone (the low was a torque-converter time on a different Acura, the high was Acura's time for the transmission plus radiator and hoses, a software update and alignment), and no Acura bulletin with a transmission-only time was found. GM prints a 'Transmission Replacement' time for the XT4 itself, 12.3 hours. That is high beside the truck's 5.4-7.4 hours, but it sits with the other transverse crossover figures loaded as cross-checks: 10.7 hours for the GMC Terrain in the same GM program, 10.8-11.5 hours for the Infiniti JX35/QX60 (including control-module reprogramming) and 10.5-10.9 hours for the MDX (including the radiator). The MDX unit lists at $5,566, so an MDX job at Acura's larger-job time would build to roughly the same top (about $7,300) as the XT4's. Weak points in the parts figures: for the midsize and luxury classes no independent remanufacturer's price could be loaded (no listing for an Accord CVT or the GM 9-speed was found; one seller's Accord page and a second Honda dealer catalog would not load), so the low in those two classes is the discounted online price of the maker's own remanufactured unit ($3,072.15 Honda, $3,575.70 GM). The midsize class still rests on one dealer-parts retailer for both ends, and a shop that buys the unit from its local dealer may pay and charge closer to list. The luxury class now has two catalogs, but they disagree: the GM remanufactured unit shows $3,921.50 list on its own page and $3,598.81 on the same site's 2019 page, and the all-wheel-drive unit shows $5,679.25 at one catalog and $5,041.98 at the other. The luxury high is the all-wheel-drive unit at list, paired with the one time GM prints for the XT4; the program's own XT4 transmission is the front-wheel-drive one, and no separate all-wheel-drive time is printed, so the top of the luxury range may understate labor on an all-wheel-drive car. A comparable midsize CVT from an independent remanufacturer (2015-2018 Nissan Altima 3.5L) is $4,549, shown for scale only. The midsize prices are for Honda's kit for the 2023 Accord CVT, because the pages for the 2021 kit failed to load (again on 2026-11-20); the economy low is a listing for the Nissan Kicks, which Nissan's catalog shows uses the same transaxle as the 2020 Versa; the economy high is a unit Nissan's catalog labels new, though it carries an $800 core charge; the truck's two prices are for different engines (5.3L and 2.7L) with the same 8-speed. Nothing is null. Core charges: all prices are WITHOUT the core charge, which is refunded when the old transmission goes back. Where shown it was $600 (Reman-Transmission, waived for 30 days), $800 (Nissan), $1,500 (Reman-Transmission 8L90), $2,000 (GM, earlier trucks) and $4,000 (GM, the XT4 unit); the Honda page shows no core charge, which does not prove none applies at checkout; a customer whose old unit is not returnable pays it. How solid the labor times are: every class now has a manufacturer-stated time for the example vehicle itself (Nissan 7.5 hr, Honda 6.2 hr including the alignment the procedure requires, GM 5.4-7.4 hr for the truck, GM 12.3 hr for the XT4); these are warranty-type times, the low end of what shops bill. Six of the eight hour figures are for the example vehicle. The economy and midsize high ends (12 hr) are a consumer guide's general statement, not vehicle-specific; no shop-side stated time for the Versa or Accord was found. The luxury class is a single figure used at both ends, read from a loosely laid-out table. Confidence stays low because the midsize class still has only one parts source (one dealer-parts retailer, for a different model year of the kit) and no independent remanufacturer's price backs the midsize or luxury low. An estimate is never a quote and never a diagnosis.
extras: A quote often adds the refundable core charge until the old unit is returned ($600-$2,000 on the listings seen), freight for the unit ($150-$299 on the listings seen), new transmission fluid (Nissan's campaign lists 12 units of CVT fluid and Honda's bulletin 8 quarts), programming or relearning of the transmission control module (two sellers say their unit must be calibrated or reflashed before use), a cooler flush or a new transmission cooler and lines (one remanufacturer requires new coolers; Acura lists 0.9 hr extra on the MDX where an accessory cooler is fitted), new mounts, seals, exhaust and intake gaskets and one-time-use nuts, coolant, a wheel alignment where the subframe is lowered, a diagnosis fee, shop supplies and sales tax. Four-wheel-drive and all-wheel-drive vehicles take longer (GM lists up to 1.7 hr more for 4WD). A new unit from the dealer, a rebuild of the existing transmission and a used unit are different jobs with different prices and warranties.
